newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia's Suharto blames Maoists for riots.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia's Suharto blames Maoists for riots.

text.p: Indonesian President Suharto said on Friday small groups of Maoist activists were behind the country's recent riots, the official Antara news agency reported.

"They are applying the Mao Zedong theory in which they (seek to) control villages and then cities," Suharto, who rose to power after a purge of Chinese-backed Indonesian communists in the 1960s, told cooperative managers from Islamic boarding schools.

Suharto, who enlisted Islamic groups in the army-sponsored massacre of more than 500,000 communists in the 1960s, said these groups were trying to change the state foundation, replace the state ideology Pancasila and the constitution.
Pancasila promotes belief in one supreme God, justice and civility, national unity, democracy through deliberation and consensus and social justice.

"Because they are small, they have used every chance to exaggerate such issues as disparities, corruption and illegal levies," Suharto said, adding that by raising these issues they hoped to strain relations between the government and the community.

Military and Islamic leaders have said the recent riots were started by "intellectual actors" who were members of unnamed groups or "formless organisations" -- a government code word for members of the banned Indonesian Communist Party (PKI).
There have been three major ethnic and religious riots in Indonesia in the last three months. However, nobody has so far been charged with organising any of the incidents.

Lieutenant-General Syarwan Hamid, head of the military's powerful socio-political section, was quoted by the leading Kompas daily on Friday as denying accusations that the army had provoked the ethnic and religious riots.

Abdurrachman Wahid, the outspoken head of Indonesia's largest Moslem group, the 30-million strong Nahdlatul Ulama, has said he believes some of the riots, which involved Moslem mobs, were started by unnamed parties to destabilise his leadership.

Four people died after an angry mob went on the rampage in Tasikmalaya, West Java, in December, setting fire to shops, buildings and churches. The violence was apparently sparked by reports of police brutality towards a Moslem religious teacher.
